Distinguished delegates, this afternoon we will continue our consideration of Agenda Item 4 on the General Exchange of Views. We will continue and hopefully conclude our consideration on Agenda Item 7, Thank you, Mr. Chairman. On the space system-based disaster management support, we will begin and hopefully conclude our consideration on— of agenda item 8 on the recent developments in the global navigation satellite systems. And if time permits, we will begin our consideration of agenda item 9 on the space weather. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. We will then suspend the plenary so that the Working Group of the Whole can hold its second meeting today. There will be 3 technical presentations this late afternoon. Delegates are reminded that the full schedule of technical presentations is available on the session's webpage. I would like to announce that An on-paper by the Secretariat containing an overview of the Working Group of the whole request at the first meeting of the Working Group held yesterday has been prepared and is now available on the webpage of the present session. Are there any questions or comments on this proposed schedule?
No.

I see none. Distinguished delegates, I would now like to continue our consideration of Item 4 of our agenda on General Exchange of Views. I now turn to the list of speakers. The first speaker on my list is the distinguished representative of The Russian Federation. The Russian Federation, the floor is yours.

Thank you, Chairperson. Good afternoon, distinguished colleagues. We would like to make a brief statement, and the full copy of our statement has been transmitted to the Secretariat. The Russian Federation reiterates our commitment to the principles of international space law based on the 1967 Outer Space Treaty. We support the maintenance of space for peaceful purposes only and equal access to its resources for all states, regardless of their level of economic and technical development. We emphasize that this applies to all countries without exception, including the DPRK. We condemn attempts that are at variance with international law to place restrictive measures on the use of space and the development of scientific and technical capacity. We firmly believe that UN COPUROS is a unique international platform for the substantive consideration and discussion of all issues related to peaceful cooperation in outer space, and also for developing measures, multilateral measures, to address issues arising with relation to that. It's important to maintain the intergovernmental nature of COPROSE's work, making decisions on the basis of consensus, and to make joint efforts to improve the effectiveness of the activity of this committee. We see any attempts to impose unilateral approaches as counterproductive. And also doubtful concepts regarding responsible conduct in outer space. We also see these as unproductive. We're shocked that many delegations continue to try and undermine international law with a new rules-based order, and they. I'd like to mention also here the UN Charter, which is in itself an integral part of international law. At the same time, we are surprised at how some countries display their attachment to the peaceful exploration of outer space, but at the same time increase their military space budgets.

Thank you.

We reject Western mantras about so-called violations by the Russian Federation of the UN Charter in the context of the situation in Ukraine. These have nothing to do with the agenda of the STSC. Once again, we underscore the need to depoliticize the discussions within this subcommittee as regards damage and harm to Ukraine's space technologies and facilities, well, these have been used for military purposes, and this makes them into a legal target, a legitimate target at this stage of events. Chairperson, given the fast growth in the space industry and the need to manage risks, our legislation and regulations are keeping pace with international standards and international requirements. As regards our legislation, we are introducing amendments regarding space traffic management, space debris mitigation, and the safe deployment of satellites, including megaconstellations. In 2025, the Russian Federation carried out 17 successful rocket launches. placing 45 satellites into orbit. These are for social and economic purposes, scientific research, education, and commercial purposes too. We've carried out crewed spaceflight and also met our obligations with regard to the International Space Station. In 2025, we launched 2 crewed Soyuz MS rockets and 3 freight rockets, Progress MS ones. We are also developing our own Russian space station, which will become a new platform for conducting research and for testing new space technologies. Another important area of our space research and exploration program is the development of remote Earth sensing. Our RES constellation includes 20 satellites, and we're carrying out major environmental projects. We are monitoring ice melting at the Arctic. We are also working on forest fire mitigation projects. We're continuing to work on our national system of satellite communications, GONETS. It contains— it consists of 18 low-orbit space satellites. In 2025, we approved a new space national project, which includes 8 federal projects. It will include solar system exploration and other elements. As part of our international cooperation, we are developing partnerships with the People's Republic of China to create the space station on the moon. We're also working with Belarus on a broad range of projects, and with India, the UAE, and other states. We're working together with our partners in the BRICS. We're working actively within the CIS. We're also providing support to joint projects on that are where COPROS has an involvement. The Russian Federation. I would like to reiterate our commitment to non-discrimination-based cooperation on space exploration for the benefit of humanity as a whole. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished delegate from the Russian Federation for his presentations. I would now like to continue and hopefully conclude our consideration on Agenda Item 7, on the Space System-Based Disaster Management Support. The first speaker on my list is the distinguished representative of the United Kingdom. United Kingdom, the floor is yours.

Chair, distinguished delegates, thank you for this opportunity to address the committee on the subject of Space System-Based Disaster management support. The United Kingdom notes that the International Charter for Space and Major Disasters— the Charter— celebrated its 25th anniversary in October, and that exactly 25 years after becoming operational, it marked its 1,000th activation. Charter Earth observation data products inform emergency operations disaster impact assessments, communications, and provide records vital for long-term risk reduction. We encourage eligible national disaster management authorities worldwide to use the Charter's universal access program. The British Geological Survey, BGS, continues to provide technical expertise as a value-added to the Charter in support of both UK and international emergency response. This includes contributions to the charter activation for Storm Eoin in the United Kingdom in January 2025, delivered in collaboration with the Scottish Environment Protection Agency, as well as support to overseas events such as the October 2025 Hurricane Melissa in Jamaica. More recently, BGS recently produced the first landslide inventory associated with the November 2025 Sumatra monsoon, mapping more than 6,000 events to inform situational awareness and recovery planning. The United Kingdom concluded its Committee of Earth Observation Satellites, CEOS, chair year by hosting the 39th CEOS plenary in Bath under the theme Unlocking Earth Observation for Society. Working with CEOS members, the UK advanced the practical use of satellite Earth observation for public services, global stocktakes, and improved methane measurement methods supporting understanding of climate-related risks and environmental hazards. The first CEOS Earth Summit held at the plenary brought together students from 6 countries, and the launch of the CEOS Youth Hub expanded global access to EO learning resources. These activities strengthened international coordination and promoted the use of satellite data for resilience, climate action, and disaster risk management. The United Kingdom's participation in the Copernicus program reinforces our commitment to international cooperation in Earth observation and ensures continued access to vital services such as the Copernicus Emergency Management Service, supporting rapid response to floods, wildfires, droughts, and other crises across Europe and beyond. Among numerous Sentinel launches in the last year, Sentinel-1D, launched in November, will deliver all-weather, day-and-night radar imaging to bolster Europe's capability to monitor environmental risks and protect critical infrastructure. The Copernicus system is also reinforced with key capabilities from the UK's commercial EO providers, including high-resolution thermal infrared data for localized monitoring of critical infrastructure, urban heat islands, water resources, and climate impacts. The United Kingdom is home to the European Space Agency's European Center for Space Applications and Telecommunications, EXSAT. The centre includes ESA's Actionable Climate Information Section, coordinating the climate change initiative and contributing to the UK's commitment to inform positive action and support global policy and interoperability. EXSAT manages more than 80 projects linked to climate change initiatives, including 6 aimed at strengthening confidence in understanding tipping element risks and abrupt Earth system changes. In other words, risks expected to increase with higher levels of global warming. A major driver for this work is improving resilience. Outputs help enhance detection and prediction of climate-driven tipping points and improve early warning systems. The United Kingdom continues to strengthen global meteorological cooperation through the Met Office's leading role in the World Meteorological Organization. This includes contributions to early warnings for all, advances in global data exchange systems, and application of AI to improve forecasting. Through the SCDO's Weather and Climate Information Services, WISER, program, the UK supports climate resilience by helping partner countries enhance weather and climate services. As the UK representative to the European Organization for the Exploitation of Meteorological Satellites, UMETSAT. The Met Office contributes to next-generation satellite missions including the MTGS-1 and MetOp-SG series, which will deliver more accurate and timely severe weather warnings and improved environmental monitoring. The UK is also driving international investment in enhanced space weather monitoring through the European Space Agency, strengthening global forecasting, communication, and the protection of critical infrastructure. Continued international collaboration is essential to address the climate crisis and mitigate disasters, and we look forward to engaging further and working with all nations in this critical undertaking. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of UK for her statement. The next speaker on my list is the distinguished representative of Colombia— I'm sorry, of Ghana. Ghana, the floor is yours.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. Ghana attaches great importance to the use of space system-based tools in enhancing national and regional disaster risk reduction capacities.

Mr.

Chair, Ghana continues to experience the increasing impacts of climate variability, coastal erosion, flooding, sea level rise, and other natural hazards that threaten communities, critical infrastructure, livelihoods, and ecosystems. In this context, satellite-derived data and geospatial technologies play an indispensable role in early warning, hazard assessment, emergency response, and resilience planning. Ghana welcomes the work undertaken in 2025 under the UN SPIDER and underscores the importance of expanding such initiatives, particularly in developing regions where vulnerabilities are compounded by limited access to data, analytical tools, and technical capacity. Mr. Chair, through UN-SPIDER, Ghana, working jointly with Nigeria, is in the process of implementing the project entitled Enhancing Climate Resilience in Ghana and Nigeria Through Space-Based Solutions. The objective of this initiative is to strengthen disaster preparedness by developing digital twins for flood-affected urban areas combined with hands-on training for flood simulation, impact assessment, and decision support for local authorities. Ghana intends to pilot this initiative in the coastal city of Keta, covering approximately 30 square kilometers, to support responses to coastal flooding, sea level rise, and erosion. We wish to express appreciation to UNOSA for its continued support for UN SPIDER activities. In addition, digital twin and Earth observation capabilities are being explored for use across other cities and districts in Ghana to support hazard monitoring, climate-resilient urban planning, and multi-hazard early warning. Collaboration with national institutions, including our National Disaster Management Organization, the NADMO, is central to strengthening domestic decision-making, decision-supporting systems. Mr. Chair, Ghana underscores that access to data, analytical tools, and technical capacity remains a critical barrier for many developing countries in the use of space-enabled disaster management solutions. We therefore reiterate the importance of sustained international cooperation through technology transfer, B, increased access to training and capacity building, and C, improved affordability and availability of high-resolution satellite data, including on open and near real-time platforms. Mr. Chair, these measures are essential for the effective implementation of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction, the Paris Agreement, the Space 2030 Agenda, and Africa's Agenda 2063, each of which highlights the need for improved risk knowledge, predictive capacity— predictive capability, and adaptation planning. Mr. Chair, as we approach the midterm review of the Space 2030 Agenda and in preparation for UNISPACE 4 in 2027, Ghana encourages that this— that disaster risk reduction and climate resilience remain central to global space policy deliberations. The continued growth of space-based applications for disaster management represents a tangible example of how space science and technology can deliver concrete benefits to societies, particularly in the Global South.

Mr.

Chair, in conclusion, Ghana reaffirms its commitment to working with UNOSA member states and regional partners to advance the use of space system-based disaster management support and to ensure that no country is left behind in accessing the tools required for resilience and sustainable development. I thank you, Mr. Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of Ghana for her statements. The next speaker on my list is the distinguished minister of Colombia. Colombia, the floor is yours.

Muchas gracias. Thank you very much. Chair, Colombia recognizes the significant impact of space technologies on natural disaster and risk management and accordingly appeals for enhanced cooperation in order to exchange knowledge, data, and best practices related to the use of space technologies for the prevention and management of disasters. In turn, we highlight the need to promote technical training programs as well as the development of spatial infrastructure in emerging countries, ensuring thus that more countries can benefit from these essential tools when it comes to risk mitigation and protection of the global population. Risk mitigation by strengthening partnerships and using information to minimize risks makes it possible to take timely decisions that can preserve lives. Initiatives such as UN SPIDER have been crucial in order to bolster the response capacity of countries in view of emergencies caused by natural disasters. This regard, Colombia has undertaken innovative projects combining the analysis of satellite imaging with artificial intelligence in order to identify risk patterns related to active volcanoes, floods, landslides, and forest fires. In addition to these achievements, UN-SPIDER has also provided Colombia with access to a global network of space knowledge and technology that has considerably helped to improve the effectiveness of our emergency operations. Chair, Colombia ranks second globally in terms of biodiversity. Almost half of our land surface area is located within the Amazonian jungle. The early detection of forest vital— of forest fires is vital in order to preserve species that are at risk of extinction, native forests, the natural heritage of our country, and serving to mitigate environmental damage and protect communities. By implementing the National Forest Fire Satellite Detection Program, it is possible to detect critical outbreaks early on in order to ensure real-time monitoring, optimizing response efforts, and to coordinate resources efficiently. The platform integrates thermic data from more than 30 private and public satellites. It issues low-latency warnings and maps forest fires as they arise, thus providing shared real-time imagery of the fires. This makes it possible for emergency and rescue teams to prioritize the threats, to minimize false alarms, and to more effectively respond across all regions. This example highlights the need to promote joint research, which in turn supports technological innovation and sustainable solutions. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Colombia for her statements. The next speaker on my list is the distinguished representative of Indonesia. Indonesia, the floor is yours.

Chair, Indonesia emphasizes the critical role of space science and technology applications in disaster risk reduction and sustainable development. Accordingly, Indonesia has implemented a series of capacity building training activities with support from the Center for Space Science and Technology Education in Asia and the Pacific. Indonesia activities in space system-based disaster management support have focused primarily on the practical application of space-based technologies. The result of the disaster analysis derived from these activities have been formally delivered to the National Disaster Management Authority of Indonesia for further operational use, including for the flood-related disasters in 3 provinces in Sumatra, Indonesia. Indonesia continues to advance research and development on space-based disaster applications. Current projects include the detection and monitoring of land and forest fires, floods, and landslides, particularly in northern coastal Java, as well as the monitoring of volcanic activities from space. These activities are expected to enhance early warning capabilities and produce measurable outcomes in disaster risk reduction. Indonesia acknowledges the valuable knowledge sharing that has contributed to the development of robust risk-informed spatial planning. The support was provided through the workshop on multi-hazard risk assessment for risk reduction and planning held in Bangkok by UN-SPIDER, the Asian and Pacific Training Center for Information and Communication Technology for Development of the Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific, the Asian Institute of Technology, and the University of Twente in November 2025. Chair, distinguished delegates, my delegation thanks partner countries who have collaborated with Indonesia in the field of space system-based disaster management. Indonesia welcomes and looks forward to greater international cooperation to strengthen regional capacities and foster collaboration to advance our collective disaster management capabilities. I thank you, Chair.

I thank the distinguished representative of Indonesia for her statement. The next speaker on my list is the distinguished representative of the Russian Federation. The Russian Federation, the floor is yours.

Chairperson, the Russian Federation's Remote Earth Sensing, RES, satellite group produces data for the Russian Federation, but also for other countries too. These are used for emergency monitoring and prevention. As of December 2025, the Russian RES constellation includes 20 satellites of different types. This configuration allows us to receive high-resolution and broad-view space monitoring data, both optical and radar. We're planning to continue developing Russia's RES constellation. It will increase— it will be expanded by 2030, and this will enable us to carry out disaster monitoring at a greater scale. Roscosmos has developed an RES single territorially distributed information system for the receipt, analysis, and distribution of RES data, including on man-made and natural disasters. The system includes 15 terrestrial data reception points. These are located in Cuba and the Antarctic. This allows us to carry out 748 imaging sessions per day, totaling 1 terabyte. The Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations actively uses the capacity of our national satellite system to forecast and model the stages of development of man-made and natural disasters. In 2025, when we activated our system, we were able to identify more than 74,000 hotspots. These were forest fires. Of these, more than 35,000 posed a real threat. Work is ongoing to improve existing and develop new technology for thermal processing and analysis of RES data. The time lag from data request to receipt is 28 hours. We continue to develop the terrestrial infrastructure for receipt and processing of space data. This allows us to have routine monitoring of disaster risks, including in the far north of the Russian Federation. In 2025, the space monitoring system of the Ministry of Emergency Situations was activated in more than 150 incidents and disasters. We have a space experiment called Scenario in which our National Emergency Situations Center receives imagery from the International Space Station and analyzes it for risk. We have a forest fire situation monitoring system in place. We identify thermal anomalies, and then this is transmitted to Emergency response centers in our own country and in neighboring countries, including Serbia, Armenia, and Kazakhstan. Chairperson, we would like to thank UN-SPIDER for the close cooperation. We would also like to express our Thanks to the International Charter on Space and Major Disasters. In 2025, the charter was activated twice in the Russian Federation. 71 space images were received in connection with an incident involving tankers in the Straits of Kerch. There were also 12 sets of images received for the Zapadkal region. These were forest fires. The images that were received under the Charter were provided to the relevant authorities. We would like to express thanks also to our partners under the Charter for providing satellite imagery in connection with an oil spill in the Straits of Kerch. We think this kind of cooperation between states under the International Charter on Space and Major Disasters is very important. And this has been proven by the years already of cooperation. Thank you very much. fruitful cooperation. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Russian Federation for her statement. The next speaker on my list is the distinguished representative of India. India, the floor is yours.

Chair and distinguished delegates, disaster risk reduction endeavors are given utmost importance in India. For alleviating the loss of precious lives, damage to property and infrastructure, and economic burden caused by disasters. Space technology plays an important role across all phases of disaster management cycle. Indian Space Research Organization collaborates with the disaster-specific model ministries and departments in India to ensure that space-based inputs are used for effective disaster management. During 2025, the country witnessed floods, landslides, forest fires, and cyclones, in addition to lightning incidents. Chair, in 2025, India launched the Integrated Control Room for Emergency Response, the state-of-the-art facility for disaster management. The National Database for Emergency Management implemented by ISRO is a key technological component of ICERER. During 2025, the Indo-Gangetic Plains and the northeastern region of India witnessed major floods. More than 310 flood inundation maps and value-added satellite data were generated and disseminated to the users for necessary management and interventions. Updated flood hazard zone atlas of Assam prepared using flood inundation information from satellite data of 1998 to 2023 was released in June 2025. A web-based unified flood inundation forecasting system called SEAFLOOD was released by Government of India, incorporating the special flood early warning system for Godavari and Tapi basins. Using the flood early warning system implemented by Department of Space, 35 flood alerts were issued for Assam State with a success score of 85%. ISRO also realized the development of a prototype landslide alert product integrating landslide susceptibility, triggering probability, and slope deformation rate. Synergistic observation from INSAT-3DR and 3DS as well as OceanSat-3 provided valuable insights and real-time forecast guidance for tropical cyclones formed in the Indian Ocean in 2025. A lightning nowcasting system is developed with lead time up to 6 hours by assimilating InSAR 3DR/3DS data and the ground-based lightning detection data. During 2025, multiple daily detections and dissemination of active forest fire were carried out, in addition to automated identification of long-duration fire events and rapid assessment of burnt area from such events. Chair, ISRO continues to support global disaster management initiatives through the International Charter Space and Major Disaster and the Sentinel Asia. The organization successfully conducted the lead role of the charter in 2025 and is the co-chair of the Steering Committee of Sentinel Asia. ISRO provided around 250 Indian remote sensing datasets towards 75 data requests from the Charter and Sentinel Asia in 2025. ISRO also contributes to the Satellite-Aided Search and Rescue, also called SSR, program, providing operational services for India and 7 neighboring countries. During 2025, SAR supports were provided to 9 distress incidents, contributing to saving precious human lives. As on January 2026, the program has supported rescue of more than 2,400 lives across 200 SAR incidents. Chair, ISRO is open to sharing its experience and expertise on the use of space technology for disaster management support for the benefit of stakeholders from member countries. Thank you, Chair, and distinguished delegates, for your kind attention.
I thank the distinguished emissary of India for his statement. The next speaker on my list is the distinguished emissary of the Republic of Korea. The Republic of Korea, the floor is yours.

Thank you, Chair. Earth observation is one of the most prominent applications of space technology. Serving as a highly effective tool for disaster management and response. Large-scale disasters that transcend national borders cannot be managed by any single nation alone. It is only through close international cooperation and the shared utilization of remote sensing data that the global community can respond more effectively. In light of this recognition, the Republic of Korea has made substantial contributions to the global disaster response and humanitarian relief efforts by promptly providing high-resolution images captured by COMSAT series and KAS-501 to the International Charter on Space and Major Disasters. With the year 2025 marking the 25th anniversary and the 1,000th disaster activation of the International Charter, the images provided by Korea, counting 877 in 2024 and 844 in 2025, have been instrumental in addressing ongoing challenges posed by natural disasters such as wildfires in Chile, flooding in Nepal and Argentina, and an oil spill in Ecuador. Technological innovation has also become increasingly important in disaster management, particularly across private sectors where emerging technologies are being leveraged to enhance response times and effectiveness. In 2025, a Korean company, Telepix, won first place in the Earth Observatory Observation for AI Challenge organized by the International Charter and European Space Agency. And this achievement highlighted synergy between Korea's advanced AI algorithms and its precise satellite data, demonstrating their effectiveness in enhancing damage assessment during large-scale disasters such as earthquakes. The Republic of Korea will continue to strengthen international cooperation and fulfill their humanitarian mission by leveraging innovative space technologies to contribute to a safer, more resilient world.

Thank you, Chair.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Republic of Korea for her statement. The next speaker on my list is the distinguished representative of Argentina. Argentina, the floor is yours.

Thank you very much, Chair. Chair, distinguished national delegations and representatives of observer entities, before beginning this specific agenda item, my delegation would like to make an explicit reference to the fact that we have disassociated ourselves from the Pact for the Future and that we consider Agenda 2030 for Sustainable Development not to be a legally binding instrument, and therefore these frameworks are not applicable to our country. Accordingly, and in order to save speaking time, we would request that the comments made regarding the Pact for the Future and Agenda 2030 under this agenda item apply to each and every one of the pending agenda items and in working groups and action groups. Thank you. Regarding agenda item 7, we wish to underscore the importance of satellite information applications for disaster and emergency management, as well as the fundamental contribution that international cooperation makes in order to ensure that there are access mechanisms to this information for the benefit of all nations when undergoing situations that significantly impact the lives of their peoples and the socioeconomic development of their nations. Accordingly, the Argentinian Republic has been supporting efforts through its space agency, the National Space Activities Commission, CONAIE. These initiatives, which are geared towards developing applications for close cooperation with strategic, national, and international partners, in order to generate new information and consolidate their use. Given our understanding of the fundamental role of cooperative work, the L-band polarimetric SAR data gathered by the SAOCOM-1A/1B mission is made available through mechanisms such as the International Charter on Space and Major Disasters, the UN SPIDER platform, as well as the Working Group on Disasters of the Committee on Earth Observation Satellites. This is in order to help develop new applications for early warning, response, and monitoring purposes. Regarding cooperation here, we would highlight the Italian-Argentinian Emergency Management Satellite System, known as SIS-GE, in cooperation with ASI, and the COSMO-SKYMED satellites. Internationally, the issue of space information applications for research and in support of emergency and disaster management is an important point of cooperation in the inter-institutional agreements that our national agency has subscribed. In Argentina, the space agency provides support through satellite imagery and products, specialized assistance, as well as training nationally, provincially, and at the municipal level. In particular, we would note the relationship with the National integrated risk management system. Chair, finally, we underscore that space information is an invaluable tool in order to support our disaster response capacity. Therefore, we highlight the need to continue international efforts of cooperation to ensure that we can sustain research and development in order to further strengthen and broaden monitoring and early warning systems for the benefit of all peoples and sustainable socioeconomic development.

Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Argentina for her statement. The next speaker on my list is the distinguished representative of Nigeria. Nigeria, the floor is yours.

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman, distinguished delegates. The United Nations Platform for Space-Based Information for Disaster Management and Emergency Response, UN-SPIDER, was established by the United Nations General Assembly through its Resolution 6110 of, uh, on December 2006. Nigeria, through the National Space Research and Development Agency, is currently hosting the United— the UN-SPIDER Regional Support Office in Nigeria. I am delighted to inform the subcommittee that several activities were implemented in 2025. Over the years, Nigeria has shown tremendous commitment to the activities of the UN SPIDER program. In demonstration of our commitment, Nigeria renewed its commitment by renew— Nigeria renewed its commitment by renewing the UN SPIDER Regional Support Office Memorandum of Understanding in Vienna, June 2025. So I'm therefore happy to present our activities under the framework of the UN SPIDER, which include participation in the UN SPIDER International Training on New Satellite Resources for Emergency Response, Disaster Charter Mapper, and other commercial solutions in January 2025. The United Nations International Conference on Space-Based Technology for Disaster Early Warnings for All in January, also Beijing, China. Development of the spotlight presentation on drought monitoring and assessment in northern Nigeria organized by EOTETNET, DEVINET Community of Practice African Region Drought Working Group in April 2025. And we participated in the Living Planet Symposium organized by the European Space Agency, and also expert meeting organized by the UN SPIDER Regional Support Office, Bonn Center for Remote Sensing of Land Surface in Vienna, June 2025. NASA has also participated in the annual UN SPIDER RSO meeting in Vienna, June 2025. Development and launch of common anticipatory action framework for riverine floods in Nigeria. We contributed and participated in the Anticipatory Action Task Force community-level simulation in Kwogi State, Nigeria, held in June to July 2025, the validation of the National Strategy for Disaster Risk Reduction 2025 to 2030 and Action Plan 2025 to 2028 organized by National Emergency Management Agency UNEMA and United Nations Development Programme in August 2025. The flood simulation exercise that was held on 11th to 17th August 2025 in Nasarawa State— this exercise is part of Italian government-funded flood resilience project implemented by the Nigerian Red Cross Society with support from IFRC. We also participated in the webinar with UNSPIDER, data for early warning and emergency response management on 9th of September, 2025. So, Mr. Chairman, NASDA is a member of the Presidential Anticipatory Action Task Force that developed and launched an anticipatory action framework shifting from reactive disaster management to proactive flood prevention. The task force included national institutions and partners in collaboration with OCHA, other UN agencies, and the Red Cross movement. The framework targeted for the flood-prone states along the River Benue's Niger aims to reduce the human and economic tolls of climate-induced flood. In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, flooding remains a recurring challenge in Nigeria. NASA has led several space-based assessments to support water-related disaster management. In particular, flood monitoring and damage assessment in Lokoja, Kogi State, flood mapping along the rivers Benue and Niger, providing time stream flood data using Sentinel-1 SAR and Landsat imagery via Google Earth Engine. In addition, Nigeria continues to monitor flooding events linked to release from the Lagdo Dam in Nigeria. We promise to continue doing what we do and we will support all the activities of the UN on disaster management. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.
Thanks to the distinguished representative of Nigeria for her statement. The next speaker on my list is the distinguished representative of Pakistan. Pakistan, the floor is yours.

Thank you, Chair. South Asia stands at the precipice of a climate emergency. urgency. In our region, climate change and urbanization are converging to amplify threats to human security, and this is not a theoretical challenge. It is our lived reality. While Pakistan still bears the scars of the catastrophic 2022 floods, 2025 tested our resilience yet again. For the first time since 1930, we witnessed some simultaneous catastrophic flooding across our major river systems. These deluges displaced over half a million people and caused economic losses surpassing $3 billion. Chair, in the face of such existential threats, space-based technologies are vital lifelines. I am pleased to report that SPARCO's— the National Space Agency of Pakistan's Disaster Watch portal provided critical near real-time situational awareness during the 2025 crisis. Furthermore, in partnership with the National Disaster Risk Management Fund, we have operationalized the NatCat model. This probabilistic tool now shapes Pakistan's disaster risk financing strategy, ensuring that development funds are prioritized based on scientific evidence rather than conjecture. Chair, Pakistan remains a staunch advocate for multilateral cooperation. Hosting a UN SPIDER Regional Support Office is since 2010 and acting as a data analysis node for Sentinel Asia. We actively bridge the gap between space capabilities and disaster reduction. We also continue our commitment to the COSPAS SARSat program. We are currently augmenting our capabilities by deploying the Medium Altitude Earth Orbit Search and Rescue, the MEOSAR system. This upgrade will significantly enhance the speed and accuracy of our humanitarian rescue efforts. Chair, looking to the future, Pakistan has established the Space Applications Center for Climate Science to monitor essential climate variables, and in this spirit, SPARCO and UNOSA will jointly organize an international conference on leveraging space technology for early warning in the first half of 2026. We extend a sincere invitation to all distinguished delegates to join us Pakistan for this pivotal event as we move from reactive measures to proactive resilience. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Pakistan for his statement. The next speaker on my list is the distinguished representative of South Africa. South Africa, the floor is yours.

Chair, distinguished delegates, My delegation associates itself with the statement delivered on behalf of Group of 77 and China and Africa Group. We further congratulate you, Chair, and new member states that have joined UNWOSA. South Africa wishes to reaffirm its strong commitment to supporting disaster risk reduction, preparedness, response, and recovery through space-based technologies. Through our National Space Agency, we continue to play a central role in strengthening national and regional capabilities for the use of space-derived information for disaster management, and in this regard, we actively support government priorities aligned with the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction and the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. Chair, The National Disaster Management Center of South Africa, in collaboration with the International Charter for Space and Major Disasters, the Center for Remote Sensing of Land Surfaces at the University of Bonn, and the United Nations Platform for Space-Based Information for Disaster Management and Emergency Response, UNSPIDER, hosted the International Charter Space and Major Disasters Regional training course from 15 to 18 September 2025 in Pretoria, South Africa. The training course contributed to capacity building for practitioners and decision makers by strengthening technical skills related to satellite data access, analysis, and operational use of the Charter for Disaster Response, with a particular focus on floods and other natural disasters. It further enhanced awareness and effective utilization of the International Charter mechanism within the region. Chair, at the national level, South Africa has been instrumental in supporting the National System of Innovation Disaster Management Framework, particularly with respect to the flood intelligence and geospatial decision support products. In the past month, various areas in our country have been hit by floods, and SANSA provided timely satellite-derived information to support early warning, situational awareness, and impact assessment for disaster management. In conclusion, Chair, South Africa remains committed to continued cooperation with United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs, UN-SPIDER, international partners, and member states to advance the use of space science and technology in building more resilient societies.
